title: A Recipe for Thought: Why Structured Frameworks and Generative AI Are the Future of Thinking
author: Anthea Roberts · Nick Lothian · Dimitri Glazkov · a.r. Routh

dom.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment

mo.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most

kp.k: Structured frameworks give open-ended AI clearer reasoning direction
kp.d: The authors use a cooking analogy to argue that powerful tools and high-quality inputs alone do not ensure exceptional results. They characterize open-ended ChatGPT as useful but liable to produce predictable outputs without direction, whereas structured analytic frameworks make intuitive thinking explicit and guide complex problem-solving. This is a cross-domain conceptual argument, not a finding about legal services or a measured comparison of AI performance.
qs: ChatGPT is the well-stocked kitchen without a recipe: flexible, powerful, and capable of turning out useful results.
It provides options, but without clear direction, those options can blend into the predictable.
These frameworks turn intuition into explicit steps, guiding your process just as a recipe transforms an average cook into someone capable of producing something much greater.

kp.k: Codifying expertise requires skills distinct from exercising expertise
kp.d: The authors distinguish successful problem-solving from the metacognitive ability to express an expert's approach as reusable instructions. They argue that translating tacit expertise into explicit frameworks makes it accessible to policymakers, business leaders and everyday problem-solvers; being an excellent practitioner does not itself guarantee the ability to create such frameworks.
qs: Similarly, a brilliant thinker may excel at solving problems but falter when asked to codify their approach into a framework others can use.
The act of turning tacit expertise into explicit instructions unlocks broader accessibility.
Similarly, structured frameworks empower policymakers, business leaders, and everyday problem-solvers to tackle complexity with tested, repeatable methods.

kp.k: Generative AI can scale codified reasoning for nonexperts
kp.d: The authors propose a division of contributions: people with metacognitive skills create repeatable reasoning frameworks, and generative AI applies those frameworks at speed and scale. They claim this can help nonexperts navigate complexity and reach well-reasoned conclusions, presenting improved collective thinking as a transformative potential rather than a quantified outcome.
qs: Some people have the metacognitive skill to generate these repeatable reasoning recipes.
Generative AI can then take these frameworks and apply them at speed and scale, allowing many to think like a few.
Frameworks ensure that even those without expertise can follow steps, navigate complexity, and reach well-reasoned conclusions.

kp.k: Textbook generation illustrates structured orchestration across many AI calls
kp.d: As a concrete illustration, the authors describe Sam Schillace's textbook factory at Microsoft. A single sentence specifying subject and grade level initiates a program that orchestrates 600 API calls to produce a complete textbook, including its table of contents, chapters, lesson plans, questions and answers. They emphasize reuse of the same creation structure across subjects, without reporting an evaluation of textbook quality.
qs: A user inputs a single sentence about the subject and grade level of the textbook they need.
Sam’s program orchestrates 600 API calls to produce a complete textbook, adhering to a recipe for textbook creation: a table of contents, chapters, lesson plans, questions, and answers.
The specific ingredients differ depending on whether it’s a math textbook or a history one, but the recipe remains the same.

kp.k: Ongoing case studies apply frameworks to complex systems
kp.d: The authors report that Anthea and Nick at Dragonfly Thinking are working on two case studies: developing an Australian national risk assessment with John Blackburn and exploring ways to reduce tribal fighting in Papua New Guinea with Miranda Forsyth. They describe structured steps as helping identify drivers, connections, interventions and feedback loops across these different problems; these are ongoing applications, not reported completed assessments or demonstrated reductions in conflict.
qs: At [Dragonfly Thinking](https://www.dragonflythinking.net/), Anthea and Nick are currently working on two case studies applying our repeatable reasoning recipes to the topics of developing an Australian national risk assessment (with John Blackburn) and exploring ways to reduce tribal fighting in Papua New Guinea (with Miranda Forsyth).
By breaking down these challenges into structured, repeatable steps, we’re helping to uncover drivers, connections, interventions and feedback loops.

kp.k: No-code infrastructure supports creating and distributing reasoning frameworks
kp.d: The article describes Dimitri's work at Google Labs on Breadboard AI as a no-code tool under development for building repeatable reasoning frameworks easily and quickly. It attributes to him the view that non-software-engineers possess wisdom they can impart to LLMs, and argues that the future requires both useful frameworks and mechanisms for creating, collecting and distributing them.
qs: He is developing [Breadboard AI](https://breadboard-ai.web.app/) as a no code tool to allow people to build these repeatable reasoning recipes both easily and quickly.
Many people who are not software engineers have what Dimitri calls "wisdom" that they can impart into LLMs to guide their thinking.
Coming up with a way to facilitate creating, collecting and distributing thinking recipes is another.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors argue that combining structured analytic frameworks with generative AI can scale expert reasoning and improve complex problem-solving.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain article about thinking, education and policy analysis, not a claim specifically about legal services. Anthea Roberts, Nick Lothian, Dimitri Glazkov and a.r. Routh argue that open-ended AI tools offer useful capabilities but often produce predictable results without structure. Their proposed alternative codifies tacit expertise into repeatable instructions that AI can apply at speed and scale. They present this combination as a way to broaden access to expertise and potentially improve collective thinking.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their argument with a textbook-generation example, ongoing policy case studies and a no-code tool-development example rather than comparative performance measurements.
pts.d: The authors describe Sam Schillace's textbook factory as using 600 API calls to produce a textbook from a sentence specifying its subject and grade level. They report that Roberts and Lothian are applying reasoning frameworks to an Australian national risk assessment and approaches to reducing tribal fighting in Papua New Guinea, claiming that the work helps identify systems relationships. They also describe Glazkov's development of Breadboard AI to facilitate creating repeatable reasoning workflows without software-engineering expertise. These are illustrative applications and development efforts; the article does not report benchmarks, controlled comparisons or measured improvements in reasoning quality.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article combines present applications and ongoing development in 2025 with an undated prediction of broader benefits, conditional on effective frameworks and their distribution.
pts.d: The textbook factory is described as an existing application; the policy case studies and Breadboard AI are ongoing work. The authors provide no deadline for widespread transformation. Their argument depends on people being able to translate tacit expertise into explicit, usable instructions, which they distinguish from expertise itself. It also requires ways to create, collect and distribute frameworks. The broader collective benefit is expressed as potential rather than a measured outcome.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed beneficiaries are policymakers, business leaders, everyday problem-solvers, non-experts and people who can contribute expertise without programming skills.
pts.d: The authors envisage non-experts gaining access to structured methods for navigating complex problems, while people with metacognitive skills supply the frameworks. No-code tooling is presented as enabling non-software-engineers to impart their knowledge to language models. Illustrative applications concern textbook creation and policy analysis. The article does not identify effects on lawyers, legal clients, legal staffing or legal markets.
